bib.title: Introduction to NumPy (Chapter 2, Python Data Science Handbook)

question: How should data be stored and manipulated as in-memory numerical arrays in Python using NumPy?
contributions: Explains fixed-type ndarray vs Python list/int overhead
Covers array attributes, indexing, slicing, views, reshape, concatenate/split
Covers ufuncs, aggregations, broadcasting, masks, fancy indexing, sorting/partitioning, structured arrays

limits: Edition/year not printed in the chapter text; 2016 inferred from NumPy 1.11.1 output and Python 3.4 references (1st edition).
Timings are single-machine %timeit 'best of 3' with no hardware stated, from the old IPython format.

Written for NumPy 1.11 / Python 3.4: np.float_, np.complex_, np.bool_ aliases (Table 2-1) were removed in NumPy 2.0; legacy np.random.seed/RandomState/np.random.* is superseded by np.random.default_rng; plt.plot(linestyle='steps') is removed in modern Matplotlib (use drawstyle='steps'); seaborn.set() is now set_theme(); text says 'array module available since Python 3.3' and recommends NumPy >=1.8.
Array printouts show old repr (e.g. dtype=bool, 3.14159 formatting) and default int64 on the book's platform; on Windows NumPy<2 default int was int32.

Source typos: Table 2-3 labels np.mean as 'Compute median of elements'; Table 2-4 shows np.dtype('f8') == np.int64 (should be float64); the rain output label '< 0.1 inches' tests <0.2; 'Out[12]' of np.empty shows ones (arbitrary).
No guidance on memory layout (C vs Fortran order), np.einsum, matmul, np.where, or np.unique; structured arrays deferred to Pandas for real work.
practices: Replace Python loops over arrays with vectorised ufunc expressions (p.52).
Use np.sum/np.min/np.max etc. rather than built-in sum/min/max/any/all on arrays (p.60, p.74).
Use & | ~ with parentheses, not and/or, for Boolean array logic (p.74-78).
Use .copy() when a slice must not alias the original (p.46).
Use np.add.at when indices repeat in an accumulate (p.83).
Use np.partition/argpartition instead of a full sort when only k smallest are needed (p.88-90).
Use out= to avoid temporary arrays in large computations (p.57).
Use np.expm1 and np.log1p for precision at small inputs (p.55).
Use Pandas rather than structured arrays for everyday heterogeneous data (p.96).
Pass axis= to aggregations; axis names the dimension collapsed (p.60).
Be wary: assigning floats into int arrays silently truncates (p.44).

terms.definition: Vectorized operations in NumPy are implemented via ufuncs, whose main purpose is to quickly execute repeated operations on values in NumPy arrays.
a set of rules for applying binary ufuncs (addition, subtraction, multiplication, etc.) on arrays of different sizes.
